name: Durban mutton curry
summary: Fiery red mutton curry with potatoes that soak up the gravy, cooked low and slow the way KwaZulu-Natal Indian families make it.
about: Durban curry grew out of the cooking of Indian indentured labourers who arrived in Natal from 1860. It is redder, oilier and hotter than most curries, coloured by the city's own chilli-rich masala blends, and potatoes always go into the pot. It is the Sunday lunch of many Durban homes, served with rice or roti and a grated carrot salad.

ingredients.name: Mutton
ingredients.note: neck, shoulder or knuckle, cut into pieces on the bone

ingredients.name: Durban masala
ingredients.note: medium or hot; use 2 tbsp for milder

steps: Heat the oil in a large heavy-based pot over medium heat. Add the cinnamon, cardamom, star anise and bay leaves and let them sizzle for about 30 seconds, until fragrant.
Add the onions and one sprig of curry leaves and fry, stirring now and then, until the onions are soft and golden brown, 10–12 minutes.
Stir in the ginger and garlic paste and fry for 1 minute, until it smells sweet and no longer raw.
Add the mutton, turn the heat up to medium-high and stir to coat it in the onions. Fry for about 5 minutes, until the meat has lost its pink colour on the outside.

Turn the heat down to low and add the Durban masala, turmeric, ground coriander and cumin and salt. Stir well and let the spices fry with the meat for 10 minutes, stirring every couple of minutes, until the oil turns red and the masala catches slightly on the base (add a splash of water if it starts to burn).
Add the grated tomatoes, tomato paste and chillies and cook for 5 minutes, until the tomato breaks down into a thick red gravy.
Pour in 2 cups of the water, bring to the boil, then cover and simmer on low for 1 hour, stirring now and then, until the mutton is starting to become tender.

Add the potatoes and the remaining ½ cup of water, pushing them into the gravy. Cover and simmer on low for another 40–45 minutes; shake the pot rather than stirring so the potatoes stay whole. It is ready when a knife slides easily into the potatoes and the meat pulls away from the bone.

Sprinkle over the garam masala and the second sprig of curry leaves, simmer uncovered for 5 minutes, then taste for salt. The gravy should be thick enough to coat a spoon, with a slick of red oil on top; add a little hot water if it is too thick.
Scatter with fresh coriander and serve hot with rice or roti and a grated carrot salad.
prepNote: Tastes even better the next day. Cool, refrigerate for up to 2 days and reheat gently with a splash of water.
